description: Our team combines a passion for education, game design, and space exploration. We believe that learning about space should be an adventure. For the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, we are creating a comprehensive simulation that goes beyond passive learning. We are building an experience that teaches problem-solving, teamwork, and scientific literacy.
summary:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive, browser-based game where players command a small outpost on the Moon or Mars for six simulated days. Players step into the boots of an astronaut: walking across the surface, driving a rover, drilling ice, and collecting science samples. They must carefully build and manage 7 life-support modules—including solar arrays, batteries, oxygen makers, and water recyclers—to keep their crew alive through harsh dust and solar storms.

The game makes learning the core mechanic. It includes a Flight School with 18 questions across 6 scientific lessons, and a "Why did this happen?" panel that explains the causal chain every time a system fails (e.g., why a dead battery stops oxygen production). Players also face a simulated communication delay before making critical decisions, teaching them the reality of deep space operations.

Developed as a single, lightweight HTML5 file, the game runs offline on any phone or computer. It integrates real NASA data, such as citing archived DONKI solar storms and real ISS life-support statistics, to ground the gameplay in actual space science while keeping it fun and accessible for children.
details:
What it does / how it works
The player picks a landing site and a callsign, then commands an outpost for six in-game days. Each hour the simulation computes solar output (sun angle, site factor, dust, storms), power demand from active modules, and the knock-on effects on oxygen, water and food. The astronaut can walk (keyboard, WASD, or drag on touch), interact with objects (E), and drive a rover (R) that is faster, shielded and carries up to 5 ice. Building modules costs materials earned by drilling ice and collecting samples. Events fire on schedule: cargo landers, leaks, overheating batteries, dust storms, solar storms. At night the player predicts whether the battery will survive; at dawn the forecast is scored. Every failure opens a “Why did this happen?” explanation. At the end, the player receives a graded certificate and a teacher report.

Benefits

  • Teaches systems thinking: power → air → water → food → radiation are one loop.
  • Active learning: decisions have costs, failures are explained, not just punished.
  • Low barrier: no install, no account, no internet, works on a phone.
  • Assessment built in: Flight School completion, forecast accuracy, quiz score, and a shareable teacher report.
  • Accessible design: touch + keyboard, dark mode, safe-area support, readable on small screens.

Intended impact
Make life-support engineering intuitive for students before they meet it in a textbook — and give teachers a ready-made, zero-setup classroom tool that produces a learning report per student.

Tools, languages, software

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6)
  • APIs: Canvas 2D (rendering), Web Audio API (Quindar tones, feedback), Pointer Events (touch), env(safe-area-inset-*) for notched phones
  • Architecture: single self-contained .html file, no build step, no dependencies, no backend, no tracking
  • Content sources: public NASA mission information (Perseverance/MOXIE, ISS ECLSS, lunar polar ice, Mars solar irradiance)
  • Testing: scripted full-mission run + manual checks on mobile and desktop; CSP-safe event delegation

How it’s creative

  • CAPCOM as a character: Mission Control narrates the tutorial with Quindar tones, turning onboarding into a story.
  • Prediction before consequence: asking “will the battery last?” before night builds anticipation and metacognition.
  • Failure as curriculum: the “Why did this happen?” panel reframes every blackout as a lesson.
  • Physicality: footprints, a sun-following shadow, flowing power cables, wind streaks, red rings on unpowered modules — the base feels alive.
  • Report as artifact: a teacher-facing dashboard generated from play, not from a separate quiz.

Factors the team considered

  • Accuracy vs. playability: real lunar nights are ~14 days; we shortened them and said so.
  • Accessibility: mobile-first controls, large touch targets, contrast, no motion that blocks play.
  • Reliability: offline single file so it works on school Wi-Fi or no Wi-Fi.
  • Safety/CSP: removed inline handlers after a real deployment failure — buttons now use event delegation.
  • Ethics: neutral framing, no political content, clearly marked as an independent educational game, not a NASA product.
  • Classroom fit: short sessions, pause, skip-tutorial, and a per-student report
